meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Judge a man by his questions rather than by his answers'?
meta.ogDescription: It's not Voltaire. The saying paraphrases a maxim by Pierre-Marc-Gaston de Lévis, published in his Maximes et réflexions (Paris, 1808).

answer.label: Not Voltaire — actually the duc de Lévis
answer.authorDates: 1764–1830 · French aphorist, soldier & Académie française member
answer.sourceLine: The thought belongs to Pierre-Marc-Gaston, duc de Lévis, whose Maxim xviii reads “Il est encore plus facile de juger de l’esprit d’un homme par ses questions que par ses réponses” in his Maximes et réflexions sur différents sujets de morale et de politique (Paris, 1808). The popular English — “Judge a man by his questions rather than by his answers” — is a smoothed paraphrase of that maxim, and appears nowhere in Voltaire; Wikiquote lists it under Voltaire’s “Misattributed” section.

source.excerpt: Il est encore plus facile de juger de l’esprit d’un homme par ses questions que par ses réponses.
trail: Wikiquote places the quote in Voltaire’s “Misattributed” section, giving the true source as Lévis’s Maximes et réflexions (Paris, 1808), Maxim xviii.
Wikipedia’s biography of the duc de Lévis notes the saying is “often attributed to Voltaire” but is in fact a version of one of Lévis’s maxims.
WIST’s Voltaire file flags the line as misattributed and prints Lévis’s French original as the genuine source.
source.excerptNote: Lévis’s original French (Maxim xviii). A close translation is “It is even easier to judge a man’s mind by his questions than by his answers” — the circulating English drops “even easier” and “mind” and turns it into a crisp imperative.

source.rightsNote: The maxim comes from Lévis’s Maximes et réflexions, first published in Paris in 1808 — long in the public domain, as is the author, who died in 1830. The circulating English is a generic paraphrase of that public-domain French, not a protected modern translation.

author.name: Pierre-Marc-Gaston de Lévis
author.heading: About Pierre-Marc-Gaston de Lévis
author.metaLine: 1764–1830 · French duke, soldier & aphorist; Académie française
author.bio: Pierre-Marc-Gaston, duc de Lévis (1764–1830) was a French soldier, royalist politician and man of letters, elected to the Académie française in 1816. He is best remembered as an aphorist for his Maximes et réflexions sur différents sujets de morale et de politique (1808), a slim collection in the French moralist tradition. His terse maxims were later, and wrongly, absorbed into the vast pool of quotations pinned on Voltaire.

misattribution.heading: Why everyone says “Voltaire”
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook case of a pithy maxim drifting to a more famous French name. Lévis wrote a two-part comparison in 1808; the internet kept the punch and swapped the author.

items.why: Quote sites, Goodreads and image-quote culture almost universally credit Voltaire, but the wording is found nowhere in his writings. Wikiquote lists it under “Misattributed” and names Lévis as the real source.

Lévis actually wrote “Il est encore plus facile de juger de l’esprit d’un homme par ses questions que par ses réponses” — a comparative observation. The English strips it to a clean command, so even the correctly-sourced version is a loose paraphrase, per Wikipedia’s note that it is ‘a version of one maxim by Lévis’.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is genuine and traceable — it is Maxim xviii of the duc de Lévis’s Maximes et réflexions (1808), not anything Voltaire wrote.

context.heading: One maxim, two casualties of the internet
lead: Lévis published his Maximes et réflexions in 1808, a slim book of aphorisms in the French moralist tradition of La Rochefoucauld and Chamfort. Among them is Maxim xviii: judging a mind is easier by the questions it asks than by the answers it gives — a compact endorsement of curiosity as the truer index of intelligence.

Over the following two centuries the maxim shed its author. Stripped to an imperative and re-branded “Voltaire,” it now circulates as a caption on countless quote images — a reminder that a good line about asking questions rarely gets asked where it came from.
context.pull: Judge a mind by its questions — and a quote by its sources.
